english.html: in the crime of lese-majesty <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>; whence, if the fisc is excluded by the heirs ab intestato, with all the more reason it is by the testamentary heirs, who altogether extinguish the force and virtue of intestate succession <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. It is true, to say frankly <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup> how matters stand, that these allegations are more acute and subtle than true. For as to what the interpreters of Italy say, that they have never seen the testaments of those condemned to death put in difficulty: they themselves also confess that by the law such dispositions are invalid <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. And it may be, too, that they were called into doubt in the very time of those who have so written; nevertheless that did not come to their knowledge. And touching the second reason, it must be considered that the confiscation of goods is not the sole cause for which the faculty of making a testament is forbidden to those condemned to death; but there is another, and more principal: because he who is condemned to death is made a slave of the penalty <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>, and diminished in his head <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup> — that is to say, he has lost his liberty, his citizenship and his family all together; or else, retaining liberty, has lost his citizenship, as we still see today in those who are confined. And so [they are] incapable of making a testament <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>; the more so if we confess, with the greater part of the Interpreters, that the testament is of the civil law: the slave can do nothing, nay, is esteemed as a dead thing <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>. Someone will perhaps be obstinate here <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup> with Justinian, saying that he who is well born — that is to say, who is not in servitude, but of free and freeborn persons — cannot by any penalty of punishment whatever be made a slave <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>. To whom it will promptly be answered that this new constitution (as Accursius and the others commonly interpret <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>) is to be understood of those condemned to civil death, or to some other penalty short of natural death, and so of those who survive the execution of the penalty to which they are condemned, and not at all of those who are condemned to suffer natural death, that is to say the separation of body and soul <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>. notes.citation: Digest 48.19 (De poenis), l. Qui ultimo (D. 48.19.29, Gaius; the margin's vimo for vltimo)
notes.original: l. qui vimo. D. de pæ.
notes.gloss: Qui ultimo supplicio damnantur, statim et civitatem et libertatem perdunt: those condemned to the last penalty at once lose citizenship and liberty, so that the punishment anticipates death.

notes.citation: Institutes 2.17.4, § Alio quoque modo (Quibus modis testamenta infirmantur)
notes.gloss: A will duly made is undone if the testator suffers capitis deminutio.

notes.citation: Institutes 1.16 (De capitis deminutione), § Maxima (Inst. 1.16.1); Institutes 2.17.4, cited above
notes.original: P. maximde cap. diminutio. & P. alio deſſus al gué.
notes.gloss: Maxima est capitis deminutio, cum aliquis simul et civitatem et libertatem amittit — the greatest diminution of head, when liberty and citizenship are lost together, as by condemnation to the mines or the beasts; the lesser, when citizenship alone is lost, as by aqua et igni interdictio or deportation — Coras's "those who are confined".

notes.citation: Institutes 2.5 (De usu et habitatione), last §; Accursius (Accurſe) on l. 1, Digest 41.1 (De adquirendo rerum dominio); Guillaume Benoît (Benedict.; Benedictus), Repetitio in cap. Raynutius (Decretals X 3.26, De testamentis), on the word testamentum; Digest 28.1 (De testamentis), l. 1
notes.original: P. dernier de vſu & ha bita. Accurſen la l. i. D. de acq. re. do. Be nedict. au. c. Rainutius ſur ce mot teſtamentum. l. i. de teſta.
notes.gloss: That the testament is an institution of the civil law (D. 28.1.1 defines it), and that the slave, having no civil standing, is as one dead.

notes.citation: Digest 50.17 (De diversis regulis iuris antiqui), l. Quod attinet (D. 50.17.32, Ulpian); Digest 48.19 (De poenis), l. Quidam
notes.original: l. quod attinet. D. de reg iur. l. quidam D. de pan.
notes.gloss: Quod attinet ad ius civile, servi pro nullis habentur: as far as the civil law goes, slaves are held as nobody. The Quidam fragment not verified.

notes.citation: Authenticum, coll. 4, Nov. 22 (De nuptiis), c. 8, § Quod autem
notes.original: P. quod aũt de nup. coll.
notes.gloss: The iiij. that opens the next margin note belongs here: coll. iiij. Nov. 22.8 abolishes servitus poenae: no freeborn person is henceforth made a slave by condemnation to the mines.

notes.citation: Authentica Sed hodie under Code 5.16 (De donationibus inter virum et uxorem; after C. 5.16.24); Bartolus (Bartole) on l. Eius § 1, Digest 28.1 (De testamentis); Digest 17.2 (Pro socio), l. Verum § Societas (cf. D. 17.2.63, Ulpian), and Accursius's gloss there
notes.original: iiij. autent ſed hodie. C. de don. inter vir. q Bartole en la l. eius P j. D. de teſt. l. veirum P. ſocietas. & illec Accurſe D. pro ſocio.
notes.gloss: Sed hodie nemo liber ex poena servus efficitur: but today no free man is made a slave by a penalty — the authentica drawn from Nov. 22.8. The stray q after vir. is a wrong sort.
